question: What shape does the Resources migration of this story take?
context: The table resource_types, the column ResourceTypeId in two tables, one primary key, one foreign key and two indexes must get new names (AC-13): resource_schemas, ResourceSchemaId, PK_resource_schemas, FK_resource_property_definitions_resource_schemas_ResourceSchemaId, IX_resource_property_definitions_ResourceSchemaId, IX_resource_schemas_GroupId_Name. The application applies pending migrations at startup and the development database is a persistent Docker volume, so the content of this one migration decides whether an old development database starts (AC-9) and whether its Resources data survives. The developer (owner) generates the migration; the fleet only states what it must contain.

code_says.claim: No migration in the repository renames a table, column or index; the closest precedent drops and re-creates an index.
The application runs MigrateAsync for every DbContext at startup; nothing preserves or wipes data outside the migrations themselves.
The development database is the named volume postgres_data.
Names are EF defaults derived from table and property names; there are four Resources migrations, the last is 20260928111659_SoftDeleteResourceTypeUniqueIndex.
The owner already decided that development data may be wiped (allowed, not required).
code_says.evidence: story.md AC-9, out_of_scope "Preserving existing development data"

options.label: Rename in place (Recommended)
options.consequences: One new migration made only of rename operations (table, two columns, two indexes) plus re-creating the primary key and the foreign key under the new names. All development data survives; an old development database starts whatever it contains. The scaffolded migration must be checked by the developer - EF may propose drop + create instead of rename when the class and the table are renamed together - and corrected by hand if so. migration-check is expected to report REVIEW; G2b is one confirmation.

options.label: Drop and recreate tables
options.consequences: One new migration that drops the four Resources tables (schemas, property definitions, instances, property values) and creates them under the new names. All schemas and resources in every development database are lost; groups, members and users stay. No hand-checking of rename detection. migration-check is expected to report DESTRUCTIVE; G2b is one confirmation.

options.label: Reset migration history
options.consequences: The four existing Resources migrations are deleted and one new initial migration is generated with the new names; the old name disappears from the migration files too. An existing development database does NOT start until the developer drops the resources area (or the whole volume) by hand - AC-9 must be reworded to say so. Every developer machine needs the manual reset.

recommendation: Rename in place (Recommended) - it is the only option that works on any existing development database without a manual step and without losing data, it matches what the story is (a rename), and it gives the repository its first reviewed rename migration before the epic brings real data.
argument_against: The data it protects was declared disposable by the owner, so the protection buys nothing today, while this is the one option that needs a human to read and possibly hand-edit the generated migration; drop-and-recreate is correct by construction. It also leaves the old name in the historical migration files forever (only the history reset removes it).
consequences: spec.md: AC-9 wording stays (first two options) or is reworded (third); tasks.md: the developer-only migration task gets its acceptance (allowed operations); G2b question after the migration exists; AC-13 and AC-14 unchanged in all options.

question: Does the error code RESOURCE_TYPE_NAME_TAKEN in the 409 response change?
context: When a schema name is already taken in the group the API answers 409 with the body {code: "RESOURCE_TYPE_NAME_TAKEN", message: "A schema with this name already exists in the group."}. The story demands both "the same result as before" (AC-1) and "no old name in the API" (AC-6, AC-7); AC-7 speaks of messages and a search for the words "resource type" does not catch this code, so the story does not settle it.

code_says.claim: The code is an explicit literal in the Resources exception mapper, returned as a bare object (not wrapped in errors).
Two integration tests assert the literal.
The frontend never reads the code; it shows the message as a toast.
The code is not part of the generated API description (error bodies are not described there).
code_says.evidence: F-0 RISK line on swagger response schemas

options.label: Rename to RESOURCE_SCHEMA_NAME_TAKEN (Recommended)
options.consequences: The 409 body differs from today in this one value; spec.md records it as the single named exception to "same result" (AC-1); two existing tests change their expected literal. No old word remains in any response.

options.label: Keep RESOURCE_TYPE_NAME_TAKEN
options.consequences: Every response is byte-for-byte what it is today; the old word stays in one response value and one source file, and the repository-wide search for the old name gets a permanent exception.

recommendation: Rename to RESOURCE_SCHEMA_NAME_TAKEN (Recommended) - the purpose of the story is one name everywhere, no client reads the code, and this is the cheapest moment (same argument as the story itself).
argument_against: An error code is a machine identifier, exactly the kind of value clients match on; it is the only place where this "rename-only" story changes a response value that is not a human message, and AC-1 literally promises the same result.
consequences: spec.md AC-1 gets a named exception (or not); AC-7 list gets the code (or an explicit exclusion); two existing endpoint tests are updated accordingly.

question: How are the two access observations found by discovery handled in this story?
context: The story requires that access for a non-owner member and for a user of another group stays exactly as today (AC-10, AC-11) and that anything questionable in today's rules is brought to the owner instead of being silently preserved or fixed. Discovery found no path by which another group reads or changes data. It found two things inside the rules: (1) any member of a group - not only the owner - can list the group's resources including deleted ones by adding includeDeleted=true; (2) a signed-in user from another group can tell whether a schema or resource id exists: an existing foreign schema answers 403, a missing one answers 404 (read) or 400 (other operations).

code_says.claim: The instance list authorizes owner-or-member and does not look at includeDeleted; includeDeleted=true removes all query filters.
No test sends includeDeleted=true as a non-owner member.
GET schema: missing -> 404 with empty body; existing but foreign -> 403. Update/delete/create-instance/list: missing schema -> 400 "Resource type not found.", foreign -> 403.
Writes are owner-only and reads are owner-or-member on every Resources endpoint; another group always gets 403 and never data.
code_says.evidence: F-2 claim and evidence for all 10 endpoints

options.label: Preserve both, record follow-up (Recommended)
options.consequences: The rename stays behaviour-neutral. The AC-10 / AC-11 baseline records both behaviours as they are, and acceptance tests will assert them. One backlog note describes both observations for a later story.

options.label: Fix includeDeleted now
options.consequences: A non-owner member asking for deleted resources no longer gets them (exact response to be chosen in a follow-up question). This is a behaviour change inside the rename story: a new acceptance criterion, and AC-10 gets one named exception. The id-existence observation is preserved and noted.

options.label: Fix both now
options.consequences: Additionally missing and foreign ids answer the same way. Status codes of several operations change for other-group users, so AC-11 no longer means "same as today"; the story stops being a pure rename and discovery will propose splitting the access changes into their own story.

options.label: Both intended, no follow-up
options.consequences: Both behaviours are declared intended: members may see deleted resources and the 403-vs-404 difference is accepted. Baseline and tests as in the first option, no backlog note.

recommendation: Preserve both, record follow-up (Recommended) - neither observation exposes another group's data, the story explicitly excludes behaviour changes, and mixing an access change into a 90-file rename makes both harder to review.
argument_against: The acceptance tests of this story will then assert the questionable behaviour (a member CAN list deleted resources), turning a gap into documented expected behaviour, and a follow-up note that is not a scheduled story may never be done.
consequences: spec.md baseline table for AC-10..AC-12; possibly a new AC and a named exception; possibly a SPLIT proposal; a backlog note under docs/backlog/.

question: Which on-screen texts that say "type" change in this story?
context: The screens already say "schema" almost everywhere. Four visible texts still say "type": (1) the column header "Type" in the group's resources table (the column shows the schema name); (2) the empty-state sentence "Create the first schema to define a resource type."; (3) the screen-reader label "Add resource of type <schema name>" on the add button of a schema; (4) the slogan on the sign-in page "One platform for every resource type.". AC-7 covers backend messages only and AC-8 only says the screens keep working, so the story does not settle these.

code_says.claim: Column header "Type" renders the schema name of each resource.
Empty-state text and aria-label in the schemas panel.
Sign-in page slogan.
One frontend test title mentions "type" for the column.

options.label: Change 3 group-screen texts (Recommended)
options.consequences: Column header becomes "Schema"; the empty state becomes "Create the first schema to describe your resources."; the label becomes "Add resource to schema <name>". The sign-in slogan stays: there "resource type" is ordinary English, not the name of the thing.

options.label: Change all 4 texts
options.consequences: As above, and the slogan becomes "One platform for every kind of resource.". After the story the words "resource type" appear nowhere in the frontend.

options.label: Leave all texts
options.consequences: No visible change on any screen; the word "type" stays in three places of the group screen next to "schema", and the frontend search for the old name gets permanent exceptions.

recommendation: Change 3 group-screen texts (Recommended) - on the group screen "Type" and "Schema" name the same thing side by side, which is the inconsistency the story removes; the slogan is marketing copy outside the Resources screens.
argument_against: Any wording change is a visible change in a story whose journey says the owner "sees no difference"; and leaving the slogan means a search for "resource type" in the frontend still finds one hit that someone has to know is intentional.
consequences: spec.md: list of UI texts under AC-8; ui-sketch.md; one frontend test title; the repository-wide search rule of ASM-14 gets (or does not get) an exception for the slogan.

question: How does the rename travel through the delivery phases (skeleton, blind acceptance tests, behaviour)?
context: The delivery pipeline assumes new behaviour: a skeleton phase that may only touch data shapes (entities, EF configuration, command/query/result records), then the developer's migration, then acceptance tests written blind that must compile and FAIL, then a behaviour phase in which the writer may not edit tests. A rename does not fit: renaming the entity class breaks every handler (forbidden in the skeleton phase), the acceptance tests seed data through the entity and DbSet names (so they need the new internal names before the behaviour phase), and the writer cannot fix test code that stops compiling when internal names change. tasks.md must be shaped for one concrete route.

code_says.claim: skeleton-check accepts only Core/Domain, DAL, ReadModels, Exceptions and *Command/*Query/*Result/*Dto records; handlers, event handlers and the Api project are violations.
red-first-prover requires the story tests to compile and fail after the skeleton; it selects tests by the AC trait only.
The old name is in 80 backend files including every handler, data provider, test factory and test client; integration tests seed through EF and domain factories.

Database names can be changed without renaming C# members (explicit ToTable; column names are EF defaults from property names, so HasColumnName can pin or move them); JSON names follow the C# property names of request/result records.
code_says.evidence: F-4 (4): ResourceTypeConfiguration.cs:11, no HasColumnName today; F-6 (1),(3)

code_says.claim: Existing Resources tests carry AC traits of story 015 (AC-3..AC-10) that collide with this story's ids AC-6..AC-10; red-first and ac-matrix would count them as this story's tests.
code_says.evidence: grep Trait("AC",…) in backend/src/Modules/*/*.IntegrationTests: AC-6 x1, AC-7 x1, AC-8 x4, AC-9 x3, AC-10 x1; tools/fleet/ac-matrix.js:45

options.label: Two steps in one story (Recommended)
options.consequences: Step 0, before the delivery baseline: a behaviour-neutral internal rename of C# names in production and test code (entity, features, handlers, data providers, factories, test classes), with database names pinned to today's and everything a client can see untouched (routes, JSON fields, operation names, messages, error code). Proof by existing scripts: every existing test green, exported swagger identical, no pending model change. It is done by the developer or the delivery conductor, like the migration, and committed with the owner's yes. Then the standard phases carry only the visible flip: skeleton = unpin database names, developer migration (rename operations) and G2b, blind tests on the new contract, behaviour = routes, fields, messages, error code, frontend. No script is waived.

options.label: Split into two stories
options.consequences: Discovery ends with a SPLIT verdict: this story becomes the internal rename only (no visible change), a second story carries routes, fields, database and frontend. Each story is simple for the pipeline, but the business session must reshape both and the old API name lives one story longer.

options.label: One pass with waivers
options.consequences: Writer and tester rename production and test code in lockstep under the conductor; the skeleton check and red-first proof are skipped with a journaled waiver and only the final gate decides. Fewest steps, but two fleet guarantees are switched off for this story and the gate needs manual handling of the missing red-first report.

recommendation: Two steps in one story (Recommended) - it keeps the owner's one-story decision, every fleet check stays on, and the risky part (the visible flip and the migration) is small and reviewed on its own while the bulk (80 files of mechanical rename) is proven by the existing tests instead of by review.
argument_against: Step 0 is a phase the fleet does not have: nobody but the developer or the unrestricted conductor can edit production and test code together, so the largest part of the story bypasses the writer/tester separation and the review rounds; and a temporary state exists in which C# says "schema" while the database and the API still say "type".
consequences: tasks.md phase layout; who performs the internal rename; whether discovery ends with G2 or with a SPLIT verdict; handoff to session C.

question: Which name does the foreign key from resource_property_definitions to resource_schemas carry in the database, given that the name written in spec AC-13 is too long for PostgreSQL?
context: spec.md AC-13 and data-model.md expect FK_resource_property_definitions_resource_schemas_ResourceSchemaId (66 characters). PostgreSQL caps identifiers at 63 characters, so that exact name can never exist; EF Core/Npgsql already scaffolded the truncated form FK_resource_property_definitions_resource_schemas_ResourceSche~ in the generated migration (the ~ marks the truncation; the live name is the 63-character prefix). The AC-13 acceptance test will assert whatever name is decided here, and the migration file must use it.

code_says.claim: The scaffolded migration names the FK with the truncation marker.
No Resources EF configuration sets an explicit constraint name today; all PK/FK/IX names are EF defaults.
The previous FK name was 62 characters and therefore fit.

options.label: Accept the truncated default name (Recommended)
options.consequences: The FK is FK_resource_property_definitions_resource_schemas_ResourceSche (63 characters, EF default). spec.md AC-13 and data-model.md are corrected to that name; the AC-13 test asserts it; the migration keeps the scaffolded name. No code change, no migration regeneration.

options.label: Explicit shorter name via HasConstraintName
options.consequences: ResourceSchemaConfiguration sets HasConstraintName("FK_resource_property_definitions_resource_schemas") (49 characters, no truncation marker). The skeleton changes (one DAL configuration line, be-writer or conductor), the migration is removed and regenerated, then corrected to rename-only again; spec.md AC-13 and data-model.md are updated to the new name; the AC-13 test asserts it.

recommendation: Accept the truncated default name (Recommended) - it is what EF Core and PostgreSQL produce without intervention, it costs nothing now, and the name still identifies table, principal table and column unambiguously; the spec simply recorded a name that cannot exist.
argument_against: A name ending in ResourceSche is an obvious truncation artefact that every future reader will stumble over, and the story is precisely about clean names; one explicit HasConstraintName line and a regenerated migration buy a readable name for the lifetime of the schema.
consequences: spec.md AC-13 wording, data-model.md FK row, the AC-13 database-names test (T018), the migration file content (T009), possibly ResourceSchemaConfiguration (skeleton) and a regenerated migration.

question: May the tester change the cleanup step (afterEach) in frontend/src/app/features/groups/services/resources-api.service.spec.ts, even though red-first.json marks that file as a hashed, read-only acceptance test file?
context: Finding conductor-0-1 (MAJOR, route tester) is correct. The spec's afterEach calls http.verify(), which throws in the last [AC-8] test because a POST /resources/types request is still open. In vitest, a throwing afterEach in the describe block stops the parent afterEach hooks from running, so Angular's global TestBed reset never runs. The next spec file in the same worker then fails with 'Cannot configure the test module when the test module has already been instantiated'. The fix has to go in that afterEach. dedup.json says frontend specs are not listed in red-first.json and may be fixed, but that is wrong: runs/016-rename-resource-schema/tests/red-first.json:402 lists frontend/src/app/features/groups/services/resources-api.service.spec.ts in acceptance_test_files (hash_version 2, acceptance_tests_hash 5d1a71e3...). Editing the file would change the gate hash, so I did not edit it without your authorisation. Conductor note: the agent numbered this DEC-101; recorded as DEC-7 in the story sequence.

code_says.claim: The spec file is hashed as a read-only acceptance test file.
The leak comes from a throwing afterEach with no TestBed reset.
The round-0 note says the frontend specs are not in red-first.json, which contradicts the file.

options.label: REBASELINE: one edit to the afterEach of the spec (Recommended)
options.consequences: The afterEach becomes `afterEach(() => { try { http.verify(); } finally { TestBed.resetTestingModule(); } });`. No assertion, AC tag or test title changes. The 6 [AC-8] tests stay red for the same reasons: missing get/create/update/deleteResourceSchema methods, and create-instance still posting to /resources/types. The verify error still surfaces, but TestBed is reset before the next file, so the unrelated count-chip and icon-settings failures go away. The conductor must recompute acceptance_tests_hash in red-first.json after the edit.

options.label: Global TestBed reset in the frontend test setup
options.consequences: Add an unconditional `beforeEach(() => getTestBed().resetTestingModule())` in a global vitest setup file. The hash stays the same, but this changes the test environment for every spec in the repo. It is broader than what the finding names (rule: a fix changes only what the finding names), and the leaking spec stays as it is.

options.label: Leave it until the [AC-8] tests turn green
options.consequences: Once the service calls /resources/schemas and the create-instance request matches, verify() stops throwing and the leak disappears. Until then the frontend suite shows one random extra failure, which breaks the red-first proof's 'only the expected tests are red' check.

recommendation: REBASELINE: one edit to the afterEach of the spec (Recommended) - it is the minimal, local fix the finding asks for. It keeps every assertion, title and AC tag, and keeps the intended red reason. The only cost is a one-time hash recompute.
argument_against: Any edit to a blind-pass file weakens the guarantee that acceptance tests were not tuned after the implementation was seen. Option C needs no rebaseline, and the problem goes away by itself once AC-8 is implemented.
consequences: If A: the tester applies the 3-line afterEach change to resources-api.service.spec.ts in the next C5 pass, the conductor recomputes acceptance_tests_hash, and the frontend red-first proof is rerun (expected: 10 [AC-8] failures, no unrelated spec failing). If B: the tester edits the global test setup file instead. If C: conductor-0-1 is closed as won't-fix and the red-first proof tolerates the extra failure.
chosen: REBASELINE: one edit to the afterEach of the spec (Recommended)

question: How are the generated frontend API files (frontend/src/app/api/Resources.ts, data-contracts.ts) brought in line for T032: full regeneration from the re-exported swagger, or a hand replacement of only the renamed identifiers?
context: tasks.md T032 says: regenerate with swagger-typescript-api; if the output layout differs from the current files beyond the rename, replace only the renamed identifiers by hand (ASM-15). A dry run of the generator (npx swagger-typescript-api generate -p generated/swagger.base.json -o <tmp> --modular) against the CURRENT swagger reproduces the file layout exactly (http-client.ts identical), but shows that the committed files are already stale before this story: data-contracts.ts lacks MicrosoftAspNetCoreMvcProblemDetails and the newer ManagementGroups member-list DTOs (52 changed lines), ManagementGroups.ts differs by 63 lines, Resources.ts by 13. The generated client class is imported nowhere (ASM-8/ASM-9), so neither option changes behaviour; the choice is about what the story diff contains and whether the generated files are truly in line with the swagger afterwards.

code_says.claim: The generated files are not imported by any production code.
code_says.evidence: spec.md Assumptions: the generated API client class is imported nowhere and no script regenerates it (ASM-8, ASM-9)

code_says.claim: The generator reproduces the current layout; differences are content, not layout.
code_says.evidence: conductor dry run 2026-10-08: http-client.ts identical ignoring CR; data-contracts.ts 52 / ManagementGroups.ts 63 / Resources.ts 13 changed lines, all pre-existing drift (ProblemDetails, GetGroupMembers DTOs)

options.label: Full regeneration (Recommended)
options.consequences: Run the generator over the re-exported swagger and replace all files under frontend/src/app/api/. The files become exactly what the swagger says, including the pre-existing drift in ManagementGroups and the ProblemDetails type. The story diff contains those unrelated generated-file changes; reviewers see them as generated-file refresh, not behaviour. FR-011 search rules are satisfied.

options.label: Rename-only hand edit (ASM-15)
options.consequences: Only the identifiers of the Resources rename are replaced in Resources.ts and data-contracts.ts (CreateResourceTypeRequest -> CreateResourceSchemaRequest, resourceTypeId -> resourceSchemaId, route strings, method names). The story diff stays minimal, but the generated files remain stale in the unrelated parts and a later regeneration will carry that drift. FR-011 search rules are satisfied.

recommendation: Full regeneration (Recommended) - the files are generated artefacts; the only honest state of a generated file is the generator output for the current swagger, and the drift is already there regardless of this story.
argument_against: The story is a rename; pulling unrelated ManagementGroups changes into its diff blurs review and the close report, and the spec explicitly allows the rename-only path (ASM-15).
consequences: T032 execution by the conductor before fe-writer; the contents of the C3b commit; whether docs/backlog gets a note about regenerating the client regularly.
